### Early career
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jayne_Anne_Phillips&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Early career")]
In the mid-1970s, Phillips left West Virginia for California, embarking on a cross-country trip in the course of which she had numerous jobs, experiences, and encounters that would greatly influence her fiction, with its focus on lonely, lost souls and struggling survivors.
In 1976, Truck Press published her first short story collection _Sweethearts_ , for which Phillips earned a [Pushcart Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pushcart_Prize "Pushcart Prize") and the Coordinating Council of Literary Magazines Fels Award.
_Sweethearts_ was followed in 1978 by a second small-press collection, _Counting_ , issued by Vehicle Editions. _Counting_ earned Phillips greater recognition and the St. Lawrence Award.
Her next collection, _[Black Tickets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Tickets "Black Tickets")_ , published by Delacorte/[Seymour Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delacorte_Press "Delacorte Press") in 1979 when she was 26, was her first book of stories and brought her national attention as a talented and important writer. _Black Tickets_ contained three types of stories: one-page fictions, inner soliloquies, and family dramas. These stories focused on the characters' loneliness, alienation, and unsuccessful search for happiness. _Black Tickets_ is mentioned in the 2006 lectures for the Modern Scholar series installment _From Here to Infinity_ , by Professor [Michael D. C. Drout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_D._C._Drout "Michael D. C. Drout"), who refers to her style —— he asserts it had a direct influence on [William Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gibson "William Gibson")'s 1984 [cyberpunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberpunk "Cyberpunk") novel _[Neuromancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuromancer "Neuromancer")_ — as a "headlong rush of story and description".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jayne_Anne_Phillips#cite_note-4) Called "the unmistakable work of early genius" by Tillie Olsen, _Black Tickets_ was praised by [Raymond Carver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond_Carver "Raymond Carver"): "These stories of America's disenfranchised – men and women light-years away from the American Dream – are quite unlike any in our literature ... this book is a crooked beauty." _Bla
